items.snippet: Apple’s ‘Surprise and shine’ event is set for September 9, but the company already surprised us this week by launching new products in late August. Here’s why that rare move could signal big things coming at the September event. If you follow Apple closely, you start to notice patterns in the company’s calendar year. New products typically launch around March, then June brings WWDC and software unveilings, followed by a big September event, and often some October launches too. While it’s not unusual to see smaller products debut via press releases throughout the rest of the year, one thing is exceptionally rare: a late August product launch. Over the past 10 years, Apple has only once launched new hardware in August. That lone product was the iMac in 2020—but it debuted early in the month on August 4. Why don’t late August launches happen? Because having a September event right around the corner means new hardware would typically be held until then. items.snippet: Apple says while Sign in with Apple addresses will still move to a new domain, Hide My Email will stay on iCloud.com after community pushback. items.title: Hot Chips 2026: Fujitsu's Monaka CPU stacks its entire cache on a separate 5nm die and narrows to 256-bit SVE2 — 350W and 500W SKUs due in 2027
items.snippet: Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works. Fujitsu gave us a detailed look at its 144-core Monaka server CPU at Hot Chips 2026 on August 24, confirming for the first time that the Arm chip runs dual 256-bit SVE2 vector units, down from the 512-bit SVE in its A64FX predecessor, and that its entire last-level cache sits on a separate 5nm die beneath the 2nm compute die. Ryohei Okazaki, lead architect of Fujitsu's processor development team, presented the design as "a made-in-Japan CPU, specifically engineered for AI performance and power efficiency," built for what the company calls green AI data centers and subsidized by Japan's New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization. The chip ships in two SKUs: a 350W air-cooled part at 2.1 GHz base and a 500W liquid-cooled part at 2.9 GHz base, with evaluation samples available now and volume production in 2027. items.title: Edge computing vs. centralized cloud: Where should inference live?
items.snippet: AI training could be suited for centralized cloud infrastructure. However, inference presents a different case.
